extracted.intended_audience: public relations counsel, press agents, and PR practitioners (and students) preparing news/publicity for newspapers and other media
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for public relations counsel on supplying and creating newsworthy material for newspapers, radio, lectures, advertising, film, and direct-mail; includes criteria for news value, ethical obligations, medium selection, event creation, audience segmentation, and relations with editors.

rubrics_metrics.name: News as a departure from the established order
rubrics_metrics.description: News is usefully defined as 'a departure from the established order' — events that deviate from regularity attract attention (e.g., crime or an exceptional display of fidelity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by Irwin and the boiler-explosion example: commonplace deaths are less newsworthy than a freak detail (a baby carriage left undisturbed) that departs from expectation. This principle underlies reporters' instinct for what will interest audiences, though it is not an exclusive definition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness (necessary but not sufficient)
rubrics_metrics.description: Timeliness — 'fresh information of something that has lately taken place' — is ordinarily required in news, but not every timely occurrence is news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many timely events occur constantly yet never become news; timeliness must combine with other factors (interest, manifestation, significance) to create newsworthiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors enhancing news value (Irwin's four factors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Four outstanding factors increase or create news value: (1) preference to read about things we like, (2) interest grows with familiarity with subject/setting/people, (3) interest increases with effect on personal concerns, (4) interest increases with the importance of persons/activities affected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these as heuristics when framing a story: emphasize affinity/audience taste, recognizable dramatis personae, personal impact, and prominence to heighten newsworthiness. Note that these emphases can sometimes appear to contradict the 'departure from order' principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement of a definite manifestation or overt act
rubrics_metrics.description: Before events become news they usually must make themselves noticeable by some overt, definite act (bankruptcy filing, fire, collision, arrest, speech, vote, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lippmann: rumor and background knowledge are insufficient for publication (libel concerns aside); there must be a definable shape or accomplished fact on which to 'peg' a story. PR counsel should arrange or wait for such manifestations when planning publicity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know and monitor reporters' beats and news sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists watch specific institutions and locations continuously or frequently (e.g., Police Headquarters, Coroner’s Office, Supreme Courts, Stock Exchange, City Hall, District Attorney, Post Office, ship/barge offices, hospitals, morgue, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public relations counsel must understand which places generate news for particular papers and which are visited less often; use that knowledge to time and funnel information. A list of metropolitan beats is provided as a practical checklist of sources to monitor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supply and create news — the counsel as creator
rubrics_metrics.description: The public relations counsel must not only supply news but actively create newsworthy events and situations to attract press attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: hotel proprietors wiring the President to force enforcement and create a story; exhibitions or symbolic invitations (invitations sent on large bricks); launching ceremonies, corner-stone layings, banquets, demonstrations, presentations — all staged with press-carrying potential in mind. Creation must respect truth and ethics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tailor material to the particular newspaper, department, and editor
rubrics_metrics.description: Material must suit the needs of each particular newspaper and even the specific editor or department (news, women's, society, business, financial, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: What is news for one paper/department may be irrelevant to another. Present angles and facts that align with the paper's interests and the editor's sensibilities to increase pickup chances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truthfulness, accuracy, and verifiability
rubrics_metrics.description: Material furnished to the press must be truthful, accurate and verifiable; these are essential moral and technical requirements for maintaining editorial trust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors are 'suspicious and cynical' but quick to detect falsehood; one spurious item can be fatal to a counsel's reputation. The Code of Ethics acknowledges the counsel's function; avoid fabrications, unverifiable rumors, and misleading presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literary quality and professional standard of writing
rubrics_metrics.description: The writing must meet the newspaper’s standards of literary quality; stories should be prepared as carefully and accurately as if an editor had assigned a reporter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present material in publishable form: clear, well-written copy appropriate to the target department. Accurate verification and professional composition preserve the editor’s faith and improve the likelihood of publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select the appropriate medium and format for the message
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose among radio, wireless telegraph, lectures, advertising, stage, motion pictures (feature, educational, newsreel), word of mouth, direct mail, and other channels depending on objectives and audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Radio: useful for speeches, symposiums, and broadcasting events; wireless telegraph: to reach newspapers/other media; lectures: stage events that create news value and reach group leaders; advertising: paid space with dimensional control and audience selection (including cooperative advertising); film/newsreel: educational films or newsreel items for visual emphasis; direct mail: segmented outreach using geographic/professional/economic lists. Combine media where effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use staged events and ceremonies to create focal points
rubrics_metrics.description: Public meetings, demonstrations, launches, dedications, presentations, banquets, and spectacles can be arranged primarily to create a focal news event that reverberates beyond attendees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stage events to produce quotable moments, visuals, and opportunities for other media (radio broadcast, newspapers, newsreels). The event itself becomes the vehicle for dissemination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Segment and classify publics for targeted outreach
rubrics_metrics.description: Classify the audience into groups (geographical, professional, business, religious, economic position, preferences) to tailor appeals and direct-by-mail campaigns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Large organizations can use detailed lists to reach specific groups; proper segmentation is one of the most important functions of the public relations counsel for direct mail, circularizing, and targeted persuasion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cooperate with advertising and other specialists
rubrics_metrics.description: Advertising is an important adjunct; the public relations counsel should consult advertising agents for paid space strategies and may coordinate cooperative advertising among advertisers or governments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advertising controls physical space and audience selection; combine advertising with other methods to create demand or propagate ideas. In planning publicity, bring in advertising specialists to determine the most effective paid formats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain high moral obligations as an advocate (avoid the propaganda stigma)
rubrics_metrics.description: As a partisan advocate the public relations counsel must overcome public suspicion by observing high ethics; advocacy may be called 'propaganda' by opponents, so counsel must maintain moral credibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand crowd psychology and attacks on motives; persistent ethical conduct and truthful, verifiable information help a new profession become established. Remember: advocacy labeled 'education' by supporters will be called 'propaganda' by opponents — conduct and transparency matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect and cultivate the editor's trust; do not supply 'spurious goods'
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors will not deal repeatedly with counsel who supply false or shoddy material; earning and retaining the editor’s faith is essential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One significant error can be fatal to relations with editors even if the public forgets. Deliver only material that an editor would accept from a reliable reporter: verified, timely, relevant, and well-written.
